name: Brennan Center for Justice (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: everyone the work reaches (US democracy, US prisons and jails) is in the United States.
summary: The Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan law and policy institute in New York and Washington, spent $57.6 million in the year to June 2025 on research, litigation and advocacy for voting rights and fair elections, checks on presidential power, and ending mass incarceration. Three branches: its 1.1% share of the US pro-democracy field's yearly cut in the chance that the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030 (12%, cut by a twentieth), valued by the income a breakdown would cost; its 1% share of the litigation that ended the emergency tariffs in February 2026 (about 0.12% of long-run GDP restored); and its 1.6% share of the reform field's part in the fall in incarceration, valued by prisoners' wellbeing and shortened lives. With its next dollar at 32% of the average (it holds about two years of spending in liquid reserves), it comes to about 0.03 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, most of it from the tariff ruling. The result is mostly uncertainty (the Center's share of the tariff litigation, the field's effect on the breakdown risk, the years a win counts; the model's own ranges alone span over a thousandfold), and all three branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: The Brennan Center's own spending in the year to 30 June 2025 on its six programme columns, with its share of management and fundraising, split between the democracy work (Democracy, Liberty and National Security: the breakdown-risk and tariff branches) and the justice branch by their direct spending. From the audited statement of functional expenses; donated legal services are left out.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Who the work reaches: everyone governed by US democracy and paying US tariffs (democracy and tariff branches) and the people kept out of prison each year by the national decline in incarceration (justice branch).

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the work changes: the chance that US democracy breaks down, valued by the income a breakdown would cost; the income the emergency tariffs cost until the courts struck them down; and years out of prison, valued by wellbeing and the deaths that prison causes. Each counts the whole field's or the whole litigation's effect; the Center's share is in the adjustments.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's own discounts for trust in the estimate, the Brennan Center's share of its field's resources, and missing data; the canonical rows are their averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

People in the United States
rows.explainer: Everyone governed by the democracy the work defends and paying the tariffs: the shared US population figure.

rows.label: Long-run income gain from staying a democracy (share of GDP per person)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Acemoglu et al. 2019): about a fifth of income per person, what a coded reversal out of democracy costs in the long run (p. 76: reversals have effects similar to democratizations).

rows.label: Share of that gain a fall to a hybrid regime would lose
rows.explainer: The event priced below is a fall below the Economist Intelligence Unit's democracy threshold (a hybrid regime), milder than the reversals behind the shared gain: Acemoglu et al. code a country democratic while Freedom House rates it Free or Partly Free and its Polity score is positive (p. 54), and most hybrid regimes pass that test. A third of the gain (10% to 70%): the low end a hybrid regime that keeps contested elections, the high end one that slides on to a coded reversal within the years counted.

rows.label: Long-run income loss of a breakdown per person per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + gain × severity): the full long-run loss on the shared log scale, valued at $uov_per_ln_consumption; its build-up is in dem_loss_years.

rows.label: Chance the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030
rows.explainer: The risk the work reduces. Anchors: a forecasting market gives 11% (Manifold, https://manifold.markets/JZB/will-the-economist-intelligent-unit, on 14 November 2026, for the Economist Intelligence Unit classing the US as a hybrid or authoritarian regime in a report before 2030; play money, 18 holders, so a weak anchor), and V-Dem's Democracy Report 2026 records the steepest one-year fall in US democracy it has measured (https://www.v-dem.net/documents/75/V-Dem_Institute_Democracy_Report_2026_lowres.pdf, p. 33: 'Within one year, the USA's LDI score has declined by 24%'). 12%, a little above the market for the record fall, from 4% to 30% (the experts V-Dem cites who call the regime already authoritarian). Not a single event drawn as happens or not: the model counts the change in its chance, as the catastrophic-risk models count a cut in a hazard.

rows.label: Share of the routes to a breakdown that the pro-democracy field works on
rows.explainer: The field litigates, supports election officials, researches and lobbies: it acts on elections, the courts and legislation, not on voters' choices, the parties or the military. V-Dem's 2025 decline was largest in legislative constraints, civil liberties and freedom of expression (p. 33), of which the field reaches the parts that go through courts and Congress. Half, from 30% to 80%.

rows.label: Share of the outcomes on those routes that a year of the field's work decides
rows.explainer: Against what would happen without the field. Reference class: on contested US policy issues the side with more money was hardly likelier to win, and resources explained under 5% of the difference between successful and failed efforts (Baumgartner et al. 2009, read in @democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate); litigation is more decisive, since a ruling needs a suit (in 2025 courts blocked most of the elections executive order and the voter-file demands in suits the field brought; Brennan Center 2025 annual report). A tenth, from 2% to 30%.

rows.label: Relative cut in the chance from one year of the whole US pro-democracy field's work
rows.explainer: The routes the field works on × the share of their outcomes it decides: about 5%. The biggest uncertainty in the model.

rows.label: Chance a year of the field's work averts a breakdown
rows.explainer: Breakdown risk × the field's relative cut; the Brennan Center's share of the field is in dem_attribution_share.

rows.label: Years from the work until it protects an election
rows.explainer: A year's work protects the next federal elections (November 2026, then 2028): about a year after the year modelled (0 to 2).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years of the full loss averted by postponing a breakdown
rows.explainer: An averted breakdown comes, if at all, the years counted later ($win_years_counted, 2.9), so the whole path of the loss, building up linearly over @democracy.democratization_years_to_effect (25 years), shifts by that many years: each twenty-fifth of the loss starts later, and the discounted loss averted is the years counted (discounted) × the average discount over the build-up. No separate repeal hazard: the years counted already say the breakdown may come later. About 3 years of the full loss at the defaults.

source.title: Democracy Fund, Field in Focus: The State of Pro-Democracy Institutional Philanthropy (October 2023)
source.quote: By our estimate, institutional philanthropy is currently investing an average of $2.7 to $3.4 billion a year to support democracy.

rows.explainer: Institutional philanthropy gave $2.7 to $3.4 billion a year in 2021-2022 (Democracy Fund); individual donors (most of the Brennan Center's own contributions) and the growth since (funders' new pledges after 2024) come on top: $4.5 billion, from $3 billion (the institutional figure alone) to $7 billion. rows.label: Evidence adjustment for the democracy branch
rows.explainer: The income effect is a cross-country panel of mostly poorer countries applied to the US (external validity), and the risk is a thin forecast; 0.5, from 0.25 to 0.8, lower than IRAP's advocacy model (0.8), whose value of a move rests on measured consumption.

rows.label: All adjustments, democracy branch
Backlash to the democracy work, as a share of the democracy branch
rows.explainer: Litigation and campaigns against the administration can harden opposition and provoke counter-measures (state bans after local wins, attacks on nonprofits): -3%, from -10% to 0.

rows.label: Value of democracy beyond income, as a share of the democracy branch
rows.explainer: The branch counts only income; civil liberties, freedom of expression and a fair hearing matter to people's lives beyond what they earn: 15%, from 0 to 50%.

rows.label: Effect of US democracy on democracy abroad, as a share of the democracy branch
rows.explainer: V-Dem's 2026 report counts the US among the major powers now autocratizing and the West's main allies; a US breakdown would weaken support for democracy elsewhere: 10%, from 0 to 40%.

rows.label: Democracy side effects, summed (benefits and harms not modelled, democracy branch)
rows.explainer: The three shares above, each with its sign, applied in the democracy branch only.

rows.label: Long-run US GDP restored by the ruling against the emergency tariffs (share)

source.title: The Budget Lab at Yale, State of U.S. Tariffs: March 9, 2026
source.page: pp. 5-6, table 1, row 'Percent change in long-run GDP' (columns: before the ruling; 10% Section 122 expiring; extended; 15% Section 122 expiring; extended)

rows.explainer: All 2025 tariffs left US GDP 0.25% smaller in the long run before the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling that the IEEPA tariffs exceeded the president's authority; after it, 0.07% if the 10% Section 122 replacement expires after 150 days (0.18% restored, the high end), 0.13% if it is made permanent (0.12% restored, the best guess, since the administration has replaced struck tariffs under other statutes) and 0.18% for a permanent 15% rate (0.07%, the low end). GDP, not tariff revenue: the duties and refunds are transfers.

rows.label: People per year newly kept out of prison or jail by the US decline in incarceration

source.title: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Correctional Populations in the United States, 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 310413, September 2025), table 1

rows.explainer: The yearly flow of the decline (Convention 3): 2,222,500 people incarcerated in 2013 and 2,086,000 in 2019 (the same column: '2019 6,343,200 4,357,500 3,492,900 878,700 2,086,000'), 136,500 fewer over six years, 22,750 a year, the years before the pandemic that the field's spending below also comes from. High: 2013-2023 (369,600 fewer, 36,960 a year), inflated by the pandemic's releases. Low: since 2021 the incarcerated population has risen (1,776,000 in 2021, 1,852,900 in 2023), so the field's yearly gain may now be near nothing.

rows.label: Share of the decline caused by policy changes (sentencing, bail, parole, drug laws)
rows.explainer: Over 2013-2019 violent crime was about flat while property crime and arrests fell (FBI Uniform Crime Reports), routes to fewer prisoners that aren't reform; states passed justice-reinvestment, sentencing and bail laws and Congress the First Step Act (2018). 60%, from 30% to 85%, allows for the fall in property crime and arrests: no study apportions the national decline.

rows.label: Share of those policy changes owed to the reform advocacy field
rows.explainer: Against officials, budgets, courts and prosecutors elected on reform: the advocacy field (research, campaigns, coalitions across left and right) is credited with 40%, from 15% to 70%, a judgment like IRAP's advocacy model's share of the refugee programme's rebuild owed to advocacy.

rows.label: Share of each year's decline the reform field caused
Wellbeing gained per year out of prison (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for what a year in prison or jail costs in life satisfaction (1.2 points, 0.5 to 3), read by every model that counts years of incarceration averted.

rows.label: Years of life lost per year in prison

source.title: Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.quote: each additional year in prison produced a 15.6% increase in the odds of death for parolees, which translated to a 2-year decline in life expectancy for each year served in prison

rows.explainer: New York parolees, 1989-2003: 2 years of life per year served. Observational, with longer sentences going to people at higher risk anyway, so the low end is a quarter of it (0.5); high 3.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person in prison
rows.explainer: People in US prisons are mostly in their thirties and forties, with life expectancy below the general population's: 40 years left (33 to 47). Turns years of life lost into a share of a death.

rows.label: Value of a death averted at prison ages
rows.explainer: The shared value of a death at ages 15-49 (most people in prison), times the shared multiplier.

rows.label: Deaths averted per year out of prison
rows.explainer: Years of life lost over the years left: about a twentieth of a death per year in prison.

rows.label: Years from a prison-year averted until the deaths it would have caused
rows.explainer: The excess risk is 'highest upon release from prison and declined over time' (Patterson 2013), recovering over about two thirds of the time served: the rest of the sentence plus a few years after release, 3 years (1 to 8).

rows.label: Discount for the delay until the deaths
rows.explainer: The delay discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years from the work until the reforms reduce incarceration
rows.explainer: Laws and rules take effect within months to a few years of passing, and sentences shorten as cases come through: 1 year (0 to 3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years a reduction counts
rows.explainer: A reduction in incarceration is a won reform: it counts $win_years_counted years, discounted; rollbacks are a side effect below.
